lead: Combinatorics is the mathematics of counting without listing. This unit teaches the sum and product rules, permutations, combinations, pigeonhole, inclusion–exclusion, recurrence relations and generating functions. After it you can count arrangements and selections, prove existence bounds, solve common recurrences and extract coefficients.
about: The unit starts with 3.1, the sum and product rules, because every later count is built from disjoint cases and independent stages. 3.2 turns those rules into permutations, combinations and circular arrangements. 3.3 uses counting to prove that some box must be crowded, and 3.4 corrects overcounted unions with inclusion–exclusion. 3.5 introduces homogeneous and non-homogeneous recurrence relations, including characteristic roots and particular solutions. 3.6 defines ordinary generating functions, and 3.7 uses them to solve recurrences step by step. 3.8, taught by only a few universities, adds derangements and distribution problems. The chapters move from direct counting to algebraic counting.

chapters.idea: Count a set of choices by adding disjoint cases or multiplying independent stages.
chapters.depth: Sum rule for disjoint alternatives; product rule for ordered stages; tree diagrams and decision tables; simple combinatorial proofs. Some syllabi call these the addition and multiplication principles. Keep examples small and check that cases are disjoint and stages independent.

figure.title: Product then sum
figure.aria: The product path shows 4 classes, 3 quotas and 5 payment methods giving 60 orders; a preset branch of 6 gives 66 total choices.

chapters.example: An IRCTC booking form offers 4 travel classes, 3 quotas and 5 payment methods. A passenger either builds a ticket from one class, one quota and one payment method, or picks one of 6 preset tatkal combos. How many choices are there? Answer: 4 × 3 × 5 + 6 = 66.
chapters.trap: Adding choices that overlap, or multiplying choices that are not independent stages.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 set operations for disjoint unions; Unit 1 basic proof language.
chapters.leave: Detailed permutation counts to 3.2; inclusion–exclusion to 3.4.

chapters.idea: Count ordered arrangements with permutations and unordered selections with combinations.
chapters.depth: nPr = n!/(n−r)!, nCr = n!/(r!(n−r)!); with and without repetition; circular permutations (n−1)!; arrangements of multisets; identities such as C(n,r)=C(n,n−r) and combinatorial proofs. Mention permutation functions only as a link to Unit 2. Some syllabi call selections combinations and arrangements permutations.

figure.title: 4-digit PIN, distinct digits, first digit not 0
figure.aria: Four PIN slots show 9 choices for the first digit, then 9, 8 and 7 choices for the remaining distinct digits.

chapters.example: A 4-digit PIN uses four different digits from 0–9 and cannot start with 0. How many PINs exist? Also, how many ways can a student choose 3 of 10 practice questions? Answer: 9 × 9 × 8 × 7 = 4536 PINs; C(10,3) = 120 choices.
chapters.trap: Using n^r when repeats are forbidden, or forgetting that 0 cannot lead while still allowing 0 later.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 product rule; Unit 2 functions for permutation functions.
chapters.leave: Derangements to 3.8; binomial series and generating functions to 3.6.

chapters.idea: If more objects than boxes are used, some box must hold at least a computed minimum.
chapters.depth: Basic pigeonhole: N objects in k boxes means one box has at least ⌈N/k⌉ objects. Generalized form with integer arithmetic; direct and contradiction proofs; examples with months, colours and subsets. Some syllabi spell it 'pigeon hole principle'. Do not overstate: the guarantee is at least one box, not a named box.

figure.title: 7 socks into 3 colours
figure.aria: Three colour boxes hold 3, 2 and 2 socks, so one box reaches 3.

chapters.example: A drawer has red, blue and green socks. In the dark, how many socks must you take to guarantee at least three socks of one colour? Answer: 6 socks can give 2 of each colour; the 7th forces ⌈7/3⌉ = 3 of one colour.
chapters.trap: Using floor instead of ceiling, or claiming that a specific colour must reach the bound.
chapters.leave: Exact counts by inclusion–exclusion to 3.4; Ramsey-type bounds to advanced reading, not here.

chapters.idea: Correct overcounted unions by subtracting intersections and adding back higher overlaps.
chapters.depth: Two-set and three-set formulas; complement counting; applications to divisibility, forbidden positions and onto functions. State |A∪B∪C| = Σ|A| − Σ|A∩B| + |A∩B∩C|. Some syllabi write PIE. Use floor for integer ranges. Keep proofs by counting elements in each region.

figure.aria: Three overlapping circles are labelled with counts 50, 33 and 20 for numbers up to 100 divisible by 2, 3 and 5.

chapters.example: How many integers from 1 to 100 are divisible by 2, 3 or 5? Answer: 50 + 33 + 20 − 16 − 10 − 6 + 3 = 74.
chapters.trap: Forgetting to add the triple intersection back, or using n/2 without floor for ranges that do not end at a multiple.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 sum and product rules; Unit 2 set union and intersection.
chapters.leave: Derangement formula to 3.8; coefficient extraction to 3.6–3.7.

chapters.idea: A recurrence defines a sequence by earlier terms; linear recurrences are solved through a characteristic equation and a particular solution.
chapters.depth: Order, linear, constant coefficients, homogeneous and nonhomogeneous. Characteristic roots for distinct and repeated roots; particular solutions for polynomial, exponential and constant forcing; initial conditions. Fibonacci as a homogeneous example; tower of Hanoi recurrence. Some syllabi say 'linear recurrence relations' and split homogeneous and non-homogeneous. Keep degree low.

figure.title: Nonhomogeneous solution
figure.aria: The recurrence splits into a homogeneous part 3 to the n and a particular part minus 2 times 2 to the n, giving 3 to the n plus 1 minus 2 to the n plus 1.

chapters.example: Solve a_n = 3a_{n−1} + 2^n for n ≥ 1 with a_0 = 1. Answer: homogeneous root r = 3; try C2^n, giving C = −2; with a_0 = 1, a_n = 3^{n+1} − 2^{n+1}.
chapters.trap: Using the homogeneous root as a particular solution when the forcing matches it; forgetting initial conditions.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 counting for setup; Unit 1 induction for verification.
chapters.leave: Generating-function solution to 3.7; Fibonacci identities to 3.6–3.7.

chapters.idea: A generating function packs a whole sequence into one power series so sequence operations become algebra.
chapters.depth: Ordinary generating functions G(x)=Σ a_n x^n; known series 1/(1−x), 1/(1−ax), (1+x)^n; shifting, scaling and convolution; partial fractions; coefficient extraction. Mention exponential generating functions only in one line. Some syllabi use 'generating function' for ordinary GF.

figure.title: From sequence to closed form
figure.aria: The odd-number sequence is written as a power series, split into two known series, and closed to (1 plus x) over (1 minus x) squared.

chapters.example: Find the ordinary generating function of the odd numbers 1, 3, 5, 7, … Answer: Σ(2n+1)x^n = 2x/(1−x)^2 + 1/(1−x) = (1+x)/(1−x)^2.
chapters.trap: Confusing the coefficient index with the value, or thinking convergence must be checked for formal power series.
chapters.prereq: 3.2 combinations for binomial series; Unit 2 basic algebra.
chapters.leave: Solving recurrences with generating functions to 3.7; derangement generating function to 3.8, optional.

chapters.idea: Multiply a recurrence by x^n, sum over n, solve the resulting equation for G(x), then read off coefficients.
chapters.depth: Step-by-step method; handling initial terms; partial fractions; extracting coefficients from 1/(1−ax)^m. Work one first-order nonhomogeneous recurrence and one Fibonacci-style recurrence. Some syllabi call this 'solving recurrence relations using generating functions'.

figure.title: GF solution pipeline
figure.aria: The recurrence is multiplied by x to the n and summed, giving G of x, which splits into two fractions and yields a sub n equals minus 1 plus 2 times 3 to the n.

chapters.example: Solve a_n = 3a_{n−1} + 2 for n ≥ 1, a_0 = 1, using generating functions. Answer: G(x) = (1+x)/((1−x)(1−3x)) = −1/(1−x)+2/(1−3x), so a_n = −1 + 2·3^n.
chapters.trap: Summing from n=0 when the recurrence starts at n=1, or losing the a0 term.
chapters.leave: Advanced derangement generating function to 3.8; convergence theory outside scope.

chapters.idea: Derangements count permutations with no fixed point; distribution problems count placements of balls into boxes.
chapters.depth: Advanced; only a few universities teach this. Derangement formula !n = n!Σ_{k=0}^n (−1)^k/k!, recurrence D_n=(n−1)(D_{n−1}+D_{n−2}), D_1=0, D_2=1; D_4=9. Stars and bars for identical balls into distinct boxes: C(r+n−1,n−1); distinct balls into distinct boxes: n^r; onto counts by inclusion–exclusion. Keep short.

figure.title: One derangement of 4 letters
figure.aria: A letter row A, B, C, D is matched to envelope row 2, 1, 4, 3, so no letter is in its own envelope.

chapters.example: Four letters are placed into four addressed envelopes, one letter per envelope. How many placements put no letter in its correct envelope? Answer: D_4 = 9.
chapters.trap: Using n! for derangements, or treating identical balls as distinct in stars and bars.
chapters.leave: General generating functions to 3.6; group actions to Unit 4.

links: existence bounds lead to exact overlap counts
